enrichment.translation_en:
CYRANO:
No! For it is only in fairy tales
That when someone says, “**I love you!**” to the shame-stricken prince,
He feels his ugliness melt away at those sunlit words...
But you would see that I remain the same.
enrichment.larger_context_summary: In the final act, Cyrano speaks to his cousin and lifelong beloved Roxane at the convent where she has mourned Christian for years. Mortally wounded but concealing his condition, Cyrano recites Christian’s last letter; Roxane recognizes that Cyrano supplied the voice and words through which Christian courted her and realizes the depth of Cyrano’s love. As she responds with love, Cyrano invokes a fairy-tale transformation only to deny that such words can alter his own ugliness. The exchange comes too late to repair their lost life together, sharpening the stakes of recognition, regret, and impending death.
enrichment.interpretive_commentary: The cited declaration has strong truth-conditional content within the imagined fairy tale: whoever speaks it presents love for the prince as real. Its exclamation mark and metaphorically radiant, transformative effect make the moment intense, but intensity alone does not give the words a separate expressive or reflexive function. Nor does the declaration explicitly promise marriage, fidelity, or future action; any courtship consequence belongs to the relationship and narrative convention rather than to a performative undertaking encoded in the sentence. Most importantly, Cyrano is not straightforwardly declaring love here. He embeds and revoices the formula as something “someone” says in a tale, then contrasts its magical result with his supposedly unchangeable appearance. That hypothetical framing lowers neither the semantic clarity of the represented avowal nor its interpretive value: it lets Cyrano indirectly confront Roxane’s love while defensively refusing the fairy-tale hope it might offer.
